questions.stem: A 36-year-old healthy woman applying for life insurance has routine bloodwork drawn. Her electrolytes are normal but her serum creatinine returns at 1.9 mg/dL. Her physician is concerned about kidney function. The serum creatinine is used as a marker of kidney function primarily because of which property?
choices: It is actively secreted by the renal tubules in proportion to GFR
It is produced from muscle at a relatively constant daily rate
It is reabsorbed completely by the proximal tubule
It is synthesized by the liver from dietary protein
Its level is independent of muscle mass
explanations: Incorrect. Creatinine is freely filtered, and the brick does not emphasize secretion as the basis for its use as a GFR marker.

Correct. Creatinine is generated from breakdown of creatine and creatine phosphate in muscle at about 1-2% of muscle stores daily, and because muscle mass is relatively stable, production is constant so a rising SCr indicates reduced kidney function.
Incorrect. Creatinine is not significantly reabsorbed; it is excreted, which is what allows it to track GFR.
Incorrect. Urea (and thus BUN) is made in the liver from protein catabolism, not creatinine.
Incorrect. SCr does depend on muscle mass, which is why person-to-person variability limits a single value and SCr is best used to follow trends.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old frail woman with sarcopenia and a 25-year-old male bodybuilder both have a measured GFR of 90 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Compared with the bodybuilder, the elderly woman is most likely to have which serum creatinine pattern?
choices: A higher SCr because of decreased renal clearance
A lower SCr because of reduced muscle mass and creatinine production
An identical SCr because GFR fully determines SCr
An undetectable SCr because of decreased dietary protein
A markedly elevated SCr because of age alone
explanations: Incorrect. Their GFRs are equal, so renal clearance of creatinine is the same.

Correct. SCr depends on both GFR and muscle mass; the brick lists muscle mass, age (young more than old), sex (males more than females), and diet as predictors of higher SCr, so a sarcopenic elderly woman generates less creatinine and has a lower SCr.
Incorrect. SCr is not solely determined by GFR; muscle mass and other factors also influence it.
Incorrect. Dietary protein influences BUN more than SCr, and SCr would not be undetectable.
Incorrect. Age alone does not raise SCr; in fact older patients with low muscle mass tend to have lower creatinine production.

questions.stem: A healthy 20-year-old man undergoes a research evaluation that includes a directly measured glomerular filtration rate. According to the brick, what is the approximate normal GFR for a healthy 20-year-old?
explanations: Incorrect. This range corresponds to chronic kidney disease, not a healthy young adult.
Incorrect. This is below the normal range for a 20-year-old.
Incorrect. Although close to normal, this is below the value cited in the brick.
Correct. The brick states that in a healthy 20-year-old, GFR is approximately 120 to 130 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and decreases by about 10 mL/min/1.73 m^2 per decade after age 30 to 40.
Incorrect. This value exceeds normal physiologic GFR.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with no known kidney disease has a stable serum creatinine. According to the brick, after age 30 to 40, GFR is expected to decline at approximately what rate?
explanations: Incorrect. This understates the brick's stated rate of physiologic decline.
Incorrect. The brick specifies a faster decline than this.
Correct. The brick states that GFR decreases by about 10 mL/min/1.73 m^2 for every decade of life after the age of 30 to 40.
Incorrect. This rate would represent pathologic decline, not normal aging.
Incorrect. This dramatic decline is not consistent with normal physiologic aging.

questions.stem: A nephrology fellow is reviewing the historical evolution of GFR estimating equations. The 1976 Cockcroft-Gault equation is built around which set of variables, captured by the mnemonic SWAG?
explanations: Incorrect. Albumin and glucose are not part of the Cockcroft-Gault equation.

Correct. The brick states Cockcroft-Gault estimates creatinine clearance using serum creatinine, weight, age, and gender (mnemonic SWAG) and approximates GFR based on a 24-hour urine creatinine clearance.
Incorrect. These are not the inputs of Cockcroft-Gault.
Incorrect. SAGE (sex, age, gender, ethnicity) is the mnemonic for the MDRD equation, not Cockcroft-Gault.
Incorrect. These are not the variables in the equation.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has his eGFR calculated using the MDRD equation. The MDRD equation, validated against radioisotope dilution studies, uses which variables (mnemonic SAGE)?
explanations: Incorrect. Glucose and electrolytes are not MDRD variables.
Correct. The brick states MDRD (1999) used radioisotope dilution as the gold standard and improved accuracy with the variables sex, age, gender, and ethnicity (SAGE).
Incorrect. Albumin is not part of the MDRD equation.
Incorrect. These are not MDRD variables.
Incorrect. Serum creatinine, weight, age, and gender (SWAG) describes Cockcroft-Gault, not MDRD.

questions.stem: A health system is updating its electronic record to use the most current and accurate eGFR equation. According to the brick, the 2021 CKD-EPI equation differs from MDRD primarily because it:
choices: Adds body weight as a variable
Adds cystatin C as a required input
Removes ethnicity as a variable to improve equity and clinical applicability
Removes age and sex as variables
explanations: Incorrect. The brick does not state that body weight was added; CKD-EPI uses sex, age, and gender.
Incorrect. The brick does not describe cystatin C as part of CKD-EPI.
Correct. The brick states the 2021 CKD-EPI equation uses sex, age, and gender but removes ethnicity as a variable to improve equity and clinical applicability.
Incorrect. CKD-EPI continues to use age and sex.
Incorrect. CKD-EPI remains based on serum creatinine, not BUN.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease is started on a medication whose dosing guideline is based on an older pharmacokinetic study from the 1980s. According to the brick, drug dosing in CKD is often based on creatinine clearance rather than eGFR for which reason?
choices: CrCl better reflects tubular drug secretion than eGFR
eGFR cannot be calculated in patients over age 70
Many older pharmacokinetic studies were performed when Cockcroft-Gault was used, before MDRD and CKD-EPI were developed
MDRD systematically underestimates GFR in CKD
Cockcroft-Gault is more accurate than CKD-EPI for all drugs
explanations: Incorrect. The brick does not justify CrCl-based dosing on the basis of tubular secretion.
Incorrect. eGFR can be calculated regardless of age.

Correct. The brick explains that drug dosing in CKD is often based on CrCl because many older pharmacokinetic studies were performed when Cockcroft-Gault was the standard, before MDRD and CKD-EPI were developed; guidelines are gradually being converted to eGFR metrics.
Incorrect. The brick does not make this claim.
Incorrect. The brick describes CKD-EPI, not Cockcroft-Gault, as the most accurate and current equation.

questions.stem: A patient completes a 24-hour urine collection. The lab reports a urine creatinine (UCr), urine volume (V) over 24 hours, and a plasma creatinine (PCr). According to the brick, the formula for creatinine clearance in mL/min is:
explanations: Incorrect. This inverts the numerator and denominator.
Correct. The brick gives CrCl (mL/min) = (UCr × V) / (PCr × 1440), where 1440 represents the number of minutes in 24 hours.
Incorrect. This rearrangement is not the clearance formula.
Incorrect. The formula uses multiplication, not addition.
Incorrect. This rearrangement is not correct.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with melena from a bleeding gastric ulcer. Labs show BUN 55 mg/dL with a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL. According to the brick, BUN can rise without a change in GFR because of all the following EXCEPT:
explanations: Incorrect. The brick lists GI bleeding as a cause of altered BUN without GFR change.
Incorrect. The brick lists corticosteroids as a cause of altered BUN without GFR change.
Incorrect. The brick lists high protein intake as a cause of altered BUN without GFR change.
Incorrect. The brick lists liver disease as a cause of altered BUN without GFR change.
Correct. Increased GFR would lower BUN by enhancing clearance; the brick lists diet, liver disease, GI bleeding, corticosteroids, and high protein intake as causes of BUN changes independent of GFR.

questions.stem: A medical student asks why blood urea nitrogen is reported as nitrogen rather than total urea, and why it is not used as a direct measure of GFR. Based on the brick, the best explanation is that BUN:
choices: Is filtered but not reabsorbed, making it equivalent to inulin
Is measured by a urease-based assay reporting only the nitrogen portion, and serves only as a surrogate marker of uremic solutes because many solutes contribute to uremia
Is produced by skeletal muscle at a constant rate and reflects only renal clearance
Is the most sensitive marker of early glomerular disease
Reflects only protein intake and is unrelated to renal function
explanations: Incorrect. The brick does not equate BUN with inulin; it explicitly states BUN is not a direct measure of GFR.

Correct. The brick states BUN measures the nitrogen portion of urea using a urease-based assay (so it is reported as nitrogen, not total urea) and that because many solutes contribute to uremia, BUN can only serve as a surrogate marker of the uremic burden, not a measure of GFR.
Incorrect. Urea is produced by the liver from protein catabolism, not skeletal muscle.
Incorrect. Urinary albumin (ACR) is the most sensitive marker of early glomerular disease, not BUN.
Incorrect. BUN is influenced by both renal function and non-renal factors.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with dysuria and suprapubic pain. A urine dipstick is performed at point of care. According to the brick, which set of constituents can the urine dipstick directly detect?
choices: Heme, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, albumin, pH, and glucose
explanations: Correct. The brick states the urine dipstick is a sensitive screening tool capable of detecting the presence of heme, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, albumin, pH, and glucose.
Incorrect. Casts, crystals, and cellular elements require urine microscopy, not dipstick.
Incorrect. Standard electrolytes are measured by separate quantitative urine assays, not the dipstick described in the brick.
Incorrect. Urea and creatinine require quantitative chemistry, not a dipstick.
Incorrect. Differentiating leukocyte type requires microscopy.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with severe flank pain has a urinalysis that shows a urine pH of 8.5 and many magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals. According to the brick, an alkaline urine pH is most classically associated with which type of kidney stone?
choices: Struvite (infection) stones with Proteus or other urease-producing bacteria
Calcium phosphate stones from type 1 RTA
explanations: Incorrect. Calcium oxalate crystals are not specifically tied to urinary pH in the brick.
Incorrect. The brick states cystine crystals form in more acidic urine, not alkaline.
Correct. The brick emphasizes that urine pH may be high in struvite (infection) kidney stones, where Proteus or other bacteria alkalinize the urine.
Incorrect. The brick associates uric acid crystals with high serum uric acid (gout, leukemia, tumor lysis), not high urine pH.
Incorrect. The brick does not discuss type 1 RTA in the context of stones; it associates low pH with type 2 or 4 RTA.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with sickle cell anemia has a urinalysis showing a specific gravity of 1.008 regardless of hydration status. According to the brick, what does an isotonic specific gravity (around 1.008) most likely represent?
choices: Isothenuria, as can be seen in sickle cell anemia
explanations: Incorrect. Concentrated urine corresponds to a specific gravity around 1.035 (osmolality ~1220 mOsm/kg) per the brick.
Incorrect. Dilute urine has a specific gravity below 1.005 (correlating with osmolality ~100 mOsm/kg) per the brick.
Correct. The brick states a specific gravity around 1.008 is isotonic and that isothenuria is seen in sickle cell anemia.
Incorrect. Specific gravity reflects osmolality, not protein content directly.
Incorrect. Specific gravity does not diagnose glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes presents with polyuria, vomiting, and fruity breath. Her urine dipstick is positive for ketones. According to the brick, ketones (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) appear in urine in which two settings?
choices: Fanconi syndrome and acute tubular necrosis
explanations: Correct. The brick states ketones are positive when acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are present, occurring during starvation/fasting and when a diabetic patient develops diabetic ketoacidosis.
Incorrect. Hemolysis and rhabdomyolysis cause heme-positive urine without RBCs, not ketonuria.
Incorrect. These cause pyuria and WBC casts, not ketonuria.
Incorrect. These cause Bence Jones proteinuria, not ketonuria.
Incorrect. Fanconi syndrome can cause glucosuria, but ketonuria is not its hallmark per the brick.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with developmental delay has a urine dipstick that is positive for glucose despite a normal serum glucose, along with phosphaturia and aminoaciduria. According to the brick, glucose can appear in the urine of a non-diabetic patient because of:
explanations: Incorrect. Diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine but not glucosuria per the brick.

Correct. The brick states that glucose is usually negative because it is completely reabsorbed, but glucosuria can be present in diabetic patients who exceed reabsorptive capacity and in Fanconi syndrome.
Incorrect. Pyelonephritis is associated with WBC casts and pyuria, not glucosuria.
Incorrect. Sickle cell anemia is linked to isothenuria in the brick, not glucosuria.
Incorrect. Tumor lysis syndrome is linked to uric acid crystals, not glucosuria.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with painless jaundice has a urine dipstick positive for bilirubin. According to the brick, bilirubinuria most likely indicates:
choices: Active hemolysis with elevated unconjugated bilirubin
Biliary obstruction or liver dysfunction diverting conjugated bilirubin into the systemic circulation, where it is filtered by the kidney
explanations: Incorrect. Unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble and is not filtered by the kidney.

Correct. The brick states that bilirubin and urobilinogen are products of heme metabolism by the liver and that biliary obstruction or liver dysfunction can divert conjugated bilirubin into the systemic circulation, where it is filtered by the kidney and detected on UA.
Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis is associated with hematuria and dysmorphic RBCs, not bilirubinuria.
Incorrect. RTA causes pH abnormalities, not bilirubinuria.
Incorrect. Dehydration concentrates urine but does not cause true bilirubinuria.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with cola-colored urine 10 days after a sore throat. Urine microscopy shows multiple dysmorphic, donut-shaped RBCs with surface blebs (acanthocytes) and an RBC cast. According to the brick, these findings most strongly indicate disease at which site?
explanations: Incorrect. Cystitis is associated with normal-shaped RBCs from low GU tract pathology per the brick.

Correct. The brick states that dysmorphic RBCs occur in glomerular disease (their shape is distorted as they squeeze through a damaged glomerular basement membrane) and that RBC casts are pathognomonic for glomerulonephritis.
Incorrect. Prostatitis produces normal RBCs from low GU pathology, not dysmorphic forms or RBC casts.
Incorrect. Stones cause normal-shaped RBCs, not dysmorphic forms.
Incorrect. Urethral pathology produces normal RBCs from low GU sources.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the ED after being found unconscious. He has muscle pain and dark, tea-colored urine. The urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but urine microscopy shows no red blood cells. According to the brick, this combination most likely reflects:
choices: ABO transfusion reaction with intravascular RBC lysis or myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis
explanations: Correct. The brick states a positive dipstick for blood with no RBCs on microscopy can reflect lysis of RBCs during ABO transfusion reactions or myoglobin in the urine after rhabdomyolysis (both produce heme positivity without intact erythrocytes).
Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis would show dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts on microscopy, not absent RBCs.
Incorrect. Pyelonephritis is characterized by pyuria and WBC casts, not heme positivity without RBCs.
Incorrect. Stones produce normal RBCs visible on microscopy.
Incorrect. Urothelial carcinoma produces hematuria with intact RBCs.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with new fever, flank pain, and dysuria has a urinalysis showing many WBCs and WBC casts. According to the brick, WBC casts are characteristic of which intrarenal processes?
choices: Acute tubular necrosis and prerenal azotemia
Renal stones and renal cell carcinoma
explanations: Incorrect. Lower UTI produces WBCs in urine but not casts, since casts can only form within renal tubules.

Correct. The brick states WBC casts can only emerge from within the kidney (where the tubules form casts), and they occur in intrarenal inflammatory diseases including pyelonephritis and interstitial nephritis.
Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis is characterized by RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs, not WBC casts.
Incorrect. ATN is characterized by granular (muddy brown) casts and renal tubular epithelial cells.
Incorrect. Stones and tumors produce hematuria, not WBC casts.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, and a positive nitrite test on dipstick. According to the brick, a positive urinary nitrite supports a UTI caused by which type of organism, while which organism would be expected to give a NEGATIVE nitrite despite causing UTI?
explanations: Correct. The brick states that many bacteria such as E. coli, Proteus, and Klebsiella convert nitrates to nitrites, but Enterococcus does not, so Enterococcus UTIs are nitrite-negative.
Incorrect. The brick explicitly states Enterococcus does NOT convert nitrates to nitrites.
Incorrect. The brick does not name S. aureus as a nitrite converter, and E. coli is nitrite-positive.
Incorrect. The brick lists Proteus as a nitrite converter, and Candida is not discussed.
Incorrect. Klebsiella is a nitrite-positive organism per the brick, and Enterococcus is nitrite-negative.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man is found unresponsive after drinking a sweet-smelling automotive fluid. Urinalysis shows numerous envelope-shaped and needle-shaped crystals. According to the brick, these crystals are most consistent with which substance, and which other condition shares this crystal type?
choices: Calcium oxalate crystals; seen in kidney stones or ethylene glycol intoxication
Struvite crystals; seen in chronic urinary infection
Uric acid crystals; seen in tumor lysis syndrome
Cholesterol crystals; seen in nephrotic syndrome
explanations: Correct. The brick states calcium oxalate crystals can occur in monohydrate (dumbbells or needles) or dihydrate (envelopes) forms and are seen in kidney stones or ethylene glycol intoxication.
Incorrect. Struvite crystals appear as coffin lids and are seen with chronic urinary infections.
Incorrect. Uric acid crystals often appear as rhomboids and are seen in gout, leukemia, and tumor lysis syndrome.
Incorrect. Cystine crystals are radiolucent and hexagonal, pathognomonic for cystinuria.
Incorrect. Cholesterol crystals are not described in this brick.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with a family history of recurrent kidney stones has urine microscopy revealing radiolucent, hexagonal crystals. According to the brick, this finding is pathognomonic for:
explanations: Correct. The brick states cystine crystals are rare, have a radiolucent hexagonal shape, and are pathognomonic of cystinuria; in more acidic urine, cysteine is highly insoluble and forms these crystals.
Incorrect. Ethylene glycol intoxication produces calcium oxalate crystals.
Incorrect. Gout produces uric acid crystals (often rhomboid).
Incorrect. Struvite stones produce coffin-lid-shaped crystals.
Incorrect. Tumor lysis produces uric acid crystals from elevated serum uric acid.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with multiple myeloma has a normal urinalysis (negative for protein) and a normal urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), but his urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) is markedly elevated. According to the brick, this discordance is best explained by which feature of the testing methods?
choices: ACR is more sensitive than UPCR for all proteins
UA dipstick reagent and ACR immunoassay detect albumin specifically, while UPCR detects all types of protein (including Bence Jones light chains) via turbidometry
UPCR can only be performed on a 24-hour collection
The UA dipstick is the most sensitive test for any urinary protein
ACR detects only globulins, not albumin
explanations: Incorrect. ACR is most sensitive for albumin specifically, not for all proteins.

Correct. The brick explains UA reagent and ACR immunoassay detect albumin, while UPCR uses turbidometry to detect ALL types of protein; multiple myeloma patients excrete free light chains (Bence Jones protein) that are missed by albumin-based tests but show up as elevated UPCR.
Incorrect. The brick states UPCR is performed from a single voided urine sample.
Incorrect. The brick notes the UA dipstick can miss small quantities of albuminuria and is not the most sensitive test for protein.
Incorrect. ACR specifically detects albumin via immunoassay, not globulins.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is admitted with septic shock and develops oliguric AKI. Urine microscopy demonstrates muddy-brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells (cells larger than WBCs with centrally located nuclei). According to the brick, these findings are characteristic of which diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect. The brick associates interstitial nephritis with WBC casts and possibly eosinophiluria, not granular casts and RTEs.

Correct. The brick defines ATN as an intrarenal AKI from toxic or hypoxic tubular cell necrosis, with granular (muddy-brown) casts and renal tubular epithelial cells (larger than WBCs with centrally located nuclei) as hallmarks on urine microscopy.
Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis is characterized by dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts.
Incorrect. Pyelonephritis is characterized by WBC casts.
Incorrect. Prerenal azotemia typically has a bland urinary sediment, not muddy-brown casts.
